title: Bald Eagle Staring at Camera
Keystone Species Justification: Bald Eagles help regulate populations of fish and smaller animals. They contribute to the balance of aquatic ecosystems. They are also important scavengers and help clean up the environment by consuming carrion. The Bald Eagle is a scavenger that cleans up dead animals from its environment and helps the overall health of its ecosystem by preventing the spread of disease. Bald Eagles are considered a keystone species in some regions. This means they have a disproportionate impact on their environment compared to their population size.
Conservation Status: Low and Removed From Endangered Species List
Conservation Action Taken: The banning of the pesticide DDT was critical in the recovery of the Bald Eagle. Bald Eagles are also protected under the Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act. These Acts prohibit the taking or possession of these raptors and their feathers or eggs or their nests. Its populations have recovered so significantly that the Bald Eagle was delisted in 2007. Its populations continue to increase. Post-delisting monitoring plans are in place to track this positive trend.
Implementing Organization: U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service

title: Longleaf Pine Needles
Keystone Species Justification: The loss of the historic range of longleaf pine has led to the decline of North America’s most diverse plant communities. Over 900 plant species have been documented as only occurring in the longleaf ecosystem. In some cases up to 170 species are found on a quarter-acre plot. Longleaf stands provide habitat for over 100 bird species, 170 reptiles and amphibians, and over 30 mammals. 30 of these species are classified as rare, threatened, or endangered (RTE) by the US Fish and Wildlife Service.
Conservation Status: Global Status is G5 (Secured)
Conservation Action Taken: TNC and its partners are working across nine states. Returning regular controlled burns to the ecosystem and letting natural wildfires burn through when developed areas are not at risk is helping existing forests thrive. Land acquisitions and conservation easements are knitting together large swaths of connected habitat to bolster populations of threatened and endangered species. And empowering private landowners who hold 86% of potential longleaf pine habitat to reintroduce longleaf pine trees onto their property is not only creating new forests but also generating sources of income.The long-term persistence of intact and natural stands of Longleaf Pine will depend on continued ecosystem management including prescribed fire. This will need to be implemented within the constraints of increased wildland urban interface issues, higher costs, liability concerns and human health related smoke management restrictions.
Implementing Organization: The Southern Conservation Trust; The Nature Conservancy; U.S. Department of Defense; The Alabama-Coushatta Tribe of Texas
Primary Threats to Species: Logging; eforestation are some of the primary threats to this species. Invasive Species like feral hogs and agricultural production increase with a decrease in an established fire regime also cause threats.

Keystone Species Justification: The red-cockaded Woodpecker is a keystone species in the fire-disclimax longleaf pine tree ecosystems of the southeastern United States due to its ability to excavate cavities in living pines. description: Today we are visiting a mature longleaf pine forest in search of Red-cockaded woodpeckers. They are small ladder-backed woodpeckers with a white cheek patch slightly larger than a downy woodpecker.  They are unlike other woodpeckers who nest in dead trees because red-cockaded woodpeckers create nest cavities in living trees. They even angle their nest upward to keep out rain. Each tree bleeds sap around the excavated hole and the sticky resin deters predators like rat snakes that climb up the trees. The woodpeckers forage for insects and eggs by picking through pine bark and sometimes forage with songbirds like bluebirds and brown headed nuthatches. They live in family groups and multiple generations help excavate cavities and help raise young. Their old nest cavities are used by many other species like great crested flycatchers and tufted titmice. We are thrilled to get a glimpse of this keystone species in this dwindling habitat of longleaf pine savannah!

description: The Red-Cockaded Woodpecker (RCW) is an endangered species under the U.S. Federal Government's Endangered Species Act of 1973 and makes its home amongst the longleaf pine forests of the American southeast. Biologists from Colorado State University's Center for Environmental Management of Military Lands (CEMML) are helping Fort Polk (a US Army training installation in west-central Louisiana) ensure the bird's survival. Through banding efforts that track the bird's population as well as the installation of artificial nesting cavities RCW populations have grown since the 1970's and 80's to the point that the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service is considering downlisting the species to threatened.

Their cavities are used secondarily by at least 27 species of vertebrates including small birds and mammals and herpetofauna and invertebrates.
Conservation Status: Near Threatened (IUCN) and as Threatened by the United States Fish and Wildlife Service.
Conservation Action Taken: Longleaf Pine Tree Reforestation. Conservation. Prescribed fire. Planting longleaf. Thinning dense stands. Lengthening pine timber rotations. Hardwood midstory control. RCW cavity installation and maintenance. RCW population management. Future conservation measures
Implementing Organization: US Fish and Wildlife Service; The N.C. Wildlife Resources Commission (NCWRC); Longleaf Alliance; America's Longleaf; National Fish and Wildlife Foundation
Primary Threats to Species: Habitat Fragmentation; Land Use Change; Deforestation
